entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Job.34.1-Job.4.1">Job 34:1-4   1</reference>  Then began Elihu and said:   2  Hear, ye wise men, my words, <div eID="gen8413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8414" type="x-p"/> And ye experienced ones, give ear to me!   3  For the ear trieth words, <div eID="gen8414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8415" type="x-p"/> As the palate tasteth by eating.   4  Let us find out what is right, <div eID="gen8415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8416" type="x-p"/> Let us explore among ourselves what is good. <div eID="gen8416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8417" type="x-p"/> After his first speech Elihu has made a brief pause; now since Job is silent, he begins anew. ויען ויאמר, lxx correctly, here as in all other instances where the phrase occurs: ὑπολαβὼν λέγει, taking up the word he said. The wise and the knowing (Arab. <hi type="italic">‛ulamâ</hi>), whose attention he bespeaks, are not Job and the three (Umbr., Hahn), who are indeed a party, and as such a subject for the arbitrative appearance of Elihu; also not every one capable of forming a judgment (Hirz.); but those in the circle of spectators and listeners which, as is assumed, has assembled round the disputants (Schlottm.). In <reference osisRef="Job.33.4">Job 33:4</reference> Elihu does not expressly mean his own ear, but that of the persons addressed: he establishes his summons to prove what he says by the general thought brought over from <reference osisRef="Job.12.11">Job 12:11</reference>, and as there (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.5.7">Job 5:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.11.12">Job 11:12</reference>), clothed in the form of the emblematic proverb, - that as there is a bodily, so there is also a mental organ of sense which tries its perceptions. לאכל is not intended as expressing a purpose (<hi type="italic">ad vescendum</hi>), but as a gerundive (<hi type="italic">vescendo</hi>). The phrase בּחר משׁפּט, occurring only here, signifies neither to institute a search for the purpose of decision (Schult. and others), since בחר does not signify to decide upon anything, nor to investigate a cause (Hahn), which would be נבחנה, but to test and choose what is right, δοκιμάζειν καὶ τὸ καλὸν κατέχειν, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.21">1Th 5:21</reference>, after which the parallel runs: <hi type="italic">cognoscamus inter nos</hi> (i.e., in common) <hi type="italic">quid bonum.</hi>

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Job.34.5-Job.9.5">Job 34:5-9   5</reference>  For Job hath said: “I am guiltless, “And God hath put aside my right.   6  “Shall I lie in spite of my right, “Incurable is mine arrow without transgression.”   7  Where is there a man like Job, <div eID="gen8417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8418" type="x-p"/> Who drinketh scorning like water,   8  And keepeth company with the workers of iniquity, <div eID="gen8418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8419" type="x-p"/> And walketh with wicked men,   9  So that he saith: “A man hath no profit “From entering into fellowship with God”?! <div eID="gen8419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8420" type="x-p"/> That in relation to God, thinking of Him as a punishing judge, he is righteous or in the right, i.e., guiltless (צדקתּי with <hi type="italic">Pathach</hi> in pause, according to Ew. §93, <hi type="italic">c,</hi> from צדק = צדק, but perhaps, comp. <reference osisRef="Prov.24.30">Pro 24:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.102.26">Psa 102:26</reference>, because the <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi> is taken only as of the value of <hi type="italic">Zakeph</hi>), Job has said <hi type="italic">verbatim</hi> in <reference osisRef="Job.13.18">Job 13:18</reference>, and according to meaning, <reference osisRef="Job.23.10">Job 23:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.27.7">Job 27:7</reference>, and throughout; that He puts aside his right (the right of the guiltless, and therefore not of one coming under punishment): Job 27:2. That in spite of his right (על, to be interpreted, according to Schultens’ example, just like <reference osisRef="Job.10.7">Job 10:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.16.17">Job 16:17</reference>), i.e., although right is on his side, yet he must be accounted a liar, since his own testimony is belied by the wrathful form of his affliction, that therefore the appearance of wrong remains inalienably attached to him, we find in idea in <reference osisRef="Job.9.20">Job 9:20</reference> and freq. Elihu makes Job call his affliction חצּי, i.e., an arrow sticking in him, viz., the arrow of the wrath of God (on the objective <hi type="italic">suff</hi>. comp. on <reference osisRef="Job.23.2">Job 23:2</reference>), after <reference osisRef="Job.6.4">Job 6:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.16.9">Job 16:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.19.11">Job 19:11</reference>; and that this his arrow, i.e., the pain which it causes him, is incurably bad, desperately malignant without (בּלי as <reference osisRef="Job.8.11">Job 8:11</reference>) פּשׁע, i.e., sins existing as the ground of it, from which he would be obliged to suppose they had thrust him out of the condition of favour, is Job’s constant complaint (vid., e.g., Job 13:23.). Another utterance of Job closely connected with it has so roused Elihu’s indignation, that he prefaces it with the exclamation of astonishment: Who is a man like Job, i.e., where in all the world (מי as <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.23">2Sa 7:23</reference>) has this Job his equal, who ... . The attributive clause refers to Job; “to drink scorn (here: blasphemy) like water,” is, according to <reference osisRef="Job.15.16">Job 15:16</reference>, equivalent to to give one’s self up to mockery with delight, and to find satisfaction in it. ארח לחברה, to go over to any one’s side, looks like a poeticized prose expression. ללכת is a continuation of the ארח, according to Ew. §351, <hi type="italic">c</hi>, but not directly in the sense "and he goes,” but, as in the similar examples, <reference osisRef="Jer.17.10">Jer 17:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.44.19">Jer 44:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.17">2Ch 7:17</reference>, and freq., in the sense of: “he is in the act of going;” comp. on <reference osisRef="Job.36.20">Job 36:20</reference> and Hab 1:17. The utterance runs: a man does not profit, viz., himself (on the use of סכן of persons as well as of things, vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.22.2">Job 22:2</reference>), by his having joyous and familiar intercourse (בּרצתו, as little equivalent to בּרוּץ as in <reference osisRef="Ps.50.18">Psa 50:18</reference>) with God. Job has nowhere expressly said this, but certainly the declaration in <reference osisRef="Job.9.22">Job 9:22</reference>, in connection with the repeated complaints concerning the anomalous distribution of human destinies (vid., especially <reference osisRef="Job.21.7">Job 21:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.24.1">Job 24:1</reference>), are the premises for such a conclusion. That Elihu, in <reference osisRef="Job.34.7">Job 34:7</reference>, is more harsh against Job than the friends ever were (comp. e.g., the well-measured reproach of Eliphaz, <reference osisRef="Job.15.4">Job 15:4</reference>), and that he puts words into Job’s moth which occur nowhere <hi type="italic">verbatim</hi> in his speeches, is worked up by the Latin fathers (Jer., Philippus Presbyter, Beda,<note placement="foot">Philippus Presbyter was a disciple of Jerome. His <hi type="italic">Comm. in Iobum</hi> is extant in many forms, partly epitomized, partly interpolated (on this subject, vid., <hi type="italic">Hieronymi Opp. ed. Vallarsi,</hi> iii. 895ff.). The commentary of Beda, dedicated to a certain Nectarius (Vecterius), is fundamentally that of this Philippus.</note> <div eID="gen8420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8421" type="x-p"/> Gregory) in favour of their unfavourable judgment of Elihu; the Greek fathers, however, are deprived of all opportunity of understanding him by the translation of the lxx (in which μυκτηρισμόν signifies the scorn of others which Job must swallow down, comp. <reference osisRef="Prov.26.6">Pro 26:6</reference>), which here perverts everything.

Another utterance of Job closely connected with it has so roused Elihu’s indignation, that he prefaces it with the exclamation of astonishment: Who is a man like Job, i.e., where in all the world (מי as 2Sa 7:23 ) has this Job his equal, who ... . His Comm. in Iobum is extant in many forms, partly epitomized, partly interpolated (on this subject, vid., Hieronymi Opp. ed. Vallarsi, iii. 895ff.). The commentary of Beda, dedicated to a certain Nectarius (Vecterius), is fundamentally that of this Philippus. Gregory) in favour of their unfavourable judgment of Elihu; the Greek fathers, however, are deprived of all opportunity of understanding him by the translation of the lxx (in which μυκτηρισμόν signifies the scorn of others which Job must swallow down, comp. Pro 26:6 ), which here perverts everything.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Job.34.10-Job.11.10">Job 34:10-11 10</reference>  Therefore, men of understanding, hearken to me! <div eID="gen8421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8422" type="x-p"/> Far be it from god to do evil, <div eID="gen8422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8423" type="x-p"/> And the Almighty to act wrongfully. 11  No indeed, man’s work He recompenseth to him, <div eID="gen8423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8424" type="x-p"/> And according to man’s walk He causeth it to be with him. “Men of heart,” according to <hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. S. 249, comp. 254, is equivalent to noee'mones or noeeroi' (lxx συνετοὶ καρδίας). The clause which Elihu makes prominent in the following reply is the very axiom which the three defend, perfectly true in itself, but falsely applied by them: evil, wrong, are inconceivable on the part of God; instead of וּלשׁדּי it is only ושׁדּי in the second member of the verse, with the omission of the <hi type="italic">praep</hi>. - a frequent form of ellipsis, particularly in Isaiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.15.8">Isa 15:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.6">Isa 28:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.48.14">Isa 48:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.61.7">Isa 61:7</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.15">Eze 25:15</reference>). Far removed from acting wickedly and wrongfully, on the contrary He practises recompense exactly apportioned to man’s deeds, and ever according to the walk of each one (ארח like דּרך or דּרכי, e.g., <reference osisRef="Jer.32.19">Jer 32:19</reference>, in an ethical sense) He causes it to overtake him, i.e., to happen to him (המציא only here and <reference osisRef="Job.37.13">Job 37:13</reference>). The general assertion brought forward against Job is now proved.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Job.34.12-Job.15.12">Job 34:12-15 12</reference>  Yea verily God acteth not wickedly, <div eID="gen8424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8425" type="x-p"/> And the Almighty perverteth not the right. 13  Who hath given the earth in charge to Him? <div eID="gen8425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8426" type="x-p"/> And who hath disposed the whole globe? 14  If He only set His heart upon Himself, <div eID="gen8426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8427" type="x-p"/> If He took back His breath and His inspiration to Himself: 15  All flesh would expire together, <div eID="gen8427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8428" type="x-p"/> And man would return to dust. <div eID="gen8428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8429" type="x-p"/> With אף אמנם (Yea verily, as <reference osisRef="Job.19.4">Job 19:4</reference>, “and really”) the counter-assertion of <reference osisRef="Job.34.11">Job 34:11</reference> is repeated, but negatively expressed (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.8.3">Job 8:3</reference>). הרשׁיע signifies sometimes to act as רשׁע, and at others to be set forth and condemned as a רשׁע; here, as the connection requires, it is the former. <reference osisRef="Job.34.13">Job 34:13</reference> begins the proof. Ewald’s interpretation: who searcheth, and Hahn's: who careth for the earth beside Him, are hazardous and unnecessary. פּקד with על of the person and the acc. of the thing signifies: to enjoin anything as a duty on any one, to entrust anything to any one, <reference osisRef="Job.36.23">Job 36:23</reference>; Num 4:27; <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.23">2Ch 36:23</reference>; therefore: who has made the earth, i.e., the care of it, a duty to Him? ארצה (<hi type="italic">Milel</hi>) is not to be refined into the meaning “to the earth” (as here by Schultens and a few others, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.1">Isa 9:1</reference> by Luzzatto: he hath smitten down, better: dishonoured, to the earth with a light stroke), but is poetically equivalent to ארץ, as לילה (comp. modern Greek ἡ νύχθα) is in prose equivalent to ליל. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.34.13">Job 34:13</reference></hi> is by no means, with Ew. and Hahn, to be translated: who observes (considers) the whole globe, שׂים as <reference osisRef="Job.34.23">Job 34:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.4.20">Job 4:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.24.12">Job 24:12</reference> - the expression would be too contracted to affirm that no one but God bestowed providential attention upon the earth; and if we have understood <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.34.13">Job 34:13</reference></hi> correctly, the thought is also inappropriate. It is worthy of remark that, according to Norzi’s statement, the Babylonian texts presented ישׁיב, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.34.14">Job 34:14</reference></hi>, as <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi>, ישׂים as <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> (like our Palestine text, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.18">Dan 11:18</reference>), which a MS of De Rossi, with a Persian translation, confirms; the reading gives a fine idea: that God’s heart is turned towards the world, and is unclosed; its ethical condition of life would then be like its physical ground of life, that God’s spirit dwells in it; the drawing back of the heart, and the taking back to Himself of the spirit, would be equivalent to the exclusion of the world from God’s love and life. However, ישׂים implies the same; for a reference of God’s thinking and willing to Himself, with the exclusion of the world, would be just a removal of His love. There is therefore a divine love which has called the world into being and keeps it in being; and this love, as the perfect opposite of sovereign caprice, is a pledge for the absolute righteousness of the divine rule.

entries.content_plain: Job 34:16-20 16 And oh understand now, hear this; Hearken to the sound of my words. 17 Would one who hateth right also be able to subdue? Or wilt thou condemn the All-just? 18 Is it becoming to say to a king: Worthless One!? Thou evil-doer! to princes? 19 To Him who accepteth not the person of rulers, And regardeth not the noble before the poor: For they are all the work of His hands. 20 In a moment they die, and at midnight The people are overthrown and perish, And they put aside the mighty - not by the hand of man. This strophe contains several grammatical rarities. At first sight it appears that Job 34:16 ought to be translated: “and if there is understanding (viz., to thee = if thou hast), then hear this.” But בּינה is accented as Milel and with Mercha , and can therefore not be a substantive (Hirz., Hahn, and others); for the retreat of the accent would be absolutely incomprehensible, and instead of a conjunctive, a distinctive, viz., Dechî , ought to be expected. Several of the old expositors, therefore, interpret with Nolde: quod quum ita sit, intellige; but this elliptical ואם, well as it might also be used for Job 21:4 , is unsupportable; the Makkeph between the two words is also against it, which rather arises from the assumption that בּינה is the imperat., and אם as an exception, like Gen 23:13 , is an optative particle joined to the imper . 2 instead of to the fut.: “and if thou shouldst observe” (= ואם־תּבין). To translate Job 34:17 with Schultens: num iram osor judicii frenabit, is impracticable on account of the order of the words, and gives a thought that is inappropriate here. אף is a particle, and the fut . is potentialis: is it also possible that an enemy of right should govern? (חבשׁ, imperio coercere, as אצר 1Sa 9:17 , אסר Psa 105:22 ); right and government are indeed mutually conditioned, without right everything would fall into anarchy and confusion. In Job 34:17 this is applied to the Ruler of the world: or (ואם, an , as Job 8:3 ; Job 21:4 ; Job 40:9 ) wilt thou condemn the mighty just One, i.e., the All-just? As Elihu calls God שׂגּיא כח, Job 37:23 , as the Almighty, and as the Omniscient One, תּמים דּעים, Job 37:16 , so here as the All-just One, צדּיק כּבּיר. entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Job.34.24-Job.28.24">Job 34:24-28 24</reference>  He breaketh the mighty in pieces without investigation <div eID="gen8444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8445" type="x-p"/> And setteth others in their place. 25  Thus He seeth through their works, <div eID="gen8445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8446" type="x-p"/> And causeth their overthrow by night, thus they are crushed. 26  He smiteth them after the manner of evil-doers <div eID="gen8446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8447" type="x-p"/> In the sight of the public. 27  For for such purpose are they fallen away from Him <div eID="gen8447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8448" type="x-p"/> And have not considered any of His ways, 28  To cause the cry of the poor to come up to Him, <div eID="gen8448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8449" type="x-p"/> And that He should hear the cry of the needy. <div eID="gen8449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8450" type="x-p"/> He makes short work (לא־חקר for בּלא, as <reference osisRef="Job.12.24">Job 12:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.38.26">Job 38:26</reference> : without research, viz., into their conduct, which is at once manifest to Him; not: in an incomprehensible manner, which is unsuitable, and still less: <hi type="italic">innumerabiles</hi>, as Jer., Syr.) with the mighty (כּבּירים, Arab. <hi type="italic">kibâr , kubarâ</hi>), and in consequence of this (<hi type="italic">fut. consec.</hi>) sets up (<hi type="italic">constituit</hi>) others, i.e., better and worthier rulers (comp. אהר, <reference osisRef="Job.8.19">Job 8:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.55.1-Isa.13.15">Isa 55:1-13 :15</reference>), in their stead. The following לכן is not equivalent to לכן אשׁר, for which no satisfactory instance exists; on the contrary, לכן here, as more frequently, introduces not the real consequence (<reference osisRef="Job.20.2">Job 20:2</reference>), but a logical inference, something that directly follows in and with what precedes (corresponding to the Greek ἄρα, just so, consequently), comp. <reference osisRef="Job.42.3">Job 42:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.26.14">Isa 26:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.61.7">Isa 61:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.33">Jer 2:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.5.2">Jer 5:2</reference>; Zec 11:7 (vid., Köhler <hi type="italic">in loc.</hi>). The <hi type="italic">Waw</hi> of וּמי, if one marks off the periods of the paratactic expression, is in both cases the <hi type="italic">Waw</hi> of conclusion after hypothetical antecedents, and. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.34.29">Job 34:29</reference></hi> refers to Job’s impetuous challenging of God. (= האמר), be it in the sense of להאמר, <hi type="italic">dicendum est</hi> (Rosenm., Schlottm., and others, after Raschi), or even in the unheard-of reflexive signification: express thyself (Stick., Hahn), is to be rejected. The syncopated form of the <hi type="italic">infin</hi>. בּהרג, <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.15">Eze 26:15</reference>, does not serve as a palliation of this adventurous imperative. It is, on the contrary, אמר with ה <hi type="italic">interrog.,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.9">Eze 28:9</reference> האמר, and probably also העמוּר Mic 2:7 (vid., Hitz.). Thus God acts with that class of unscrupulous men who abuse their power for the destruction of their subjects: for he (one of them) says (or: has said, from the standpoint of the execution of punishment) to God, etc. Ew. differently: “for one says thus to God even: I expiate what I do not commit,” by understanding the speech quoted of a defiance which reproachfully demands an explanation. And since Elihu with כי establishes the execution of punishment from this, that it never entered the mind of the עדם חנף thus to humble himself before God, so נשׂאתי here cannot signify: I have repented (put up with and had to bear what I have deserved); on the contrary, the confession begins with the avowal: I have exalted myself (נשׂא, se efferre, in Hos 13:1; Psa 89:10 ), which is then followed by the vow: I will not (in the future) do evil (חבל synon. עוה, as Neh 1:7 , and probably also supra , Job 24:9 ), and the entreaty, Job 34:32 : beside that which I behold (elliptical object-clause, Ew. §333, b ), i.e., what lies beyond my vision (= נסתּרות or עלמים, Psa 19:13 ; Psa 90:8 , unacknowledged sins), teach me; and the present vow has reference to acknowledged sins and sins that have still to be acknowledged: if I have done wrong, I will do it no more. Thus speaking - Elihu means - those high ones might have anticipated the punishment of the All-just God, for favour instead of wrath cannot be extorted, it is only reached by the way of lowly penitence.

For thou hast found fault, <div eID="gen8456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8457" type="x-p"/> So that thou hast to determine, not I, <div eID="gen8457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8458" type="x-p"/> And what thou knowest speak out! 34  Men of understanding will say to me, <div eID="gen8458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8459" type="x-p"/> And a wise man who listeneth to me: 35  “Job speaketh without knowledge, “And his words are without intelligence.” 36  O would that Job were proved to the extreme <div eID="gen8459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8460" type="x-p"/> On account of his answers after the manner of evil men; 37  For he addeth transgression to his sin, <div eID="gen8460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8461" type="x-p"/> Among us he clappeth <div eID="gen8461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8462" type="x-p"/> And multiplieth his speeches against God. <div eID="gen8462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8463" type="x-p"/> The question put to Job, whether then from him or according to his idea (עם in מעמּך as <reference osisRef="Job.23.10">Job 23:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.27.11">Job 27:11</reference>, which see) shall God recompense it (viz., as this “it” is to be understood according to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.34.32">Job 34:32</reference></hi>: man’s evil-doing and actions in general), Elihu proves from this, that Job has despised (shown himself discontented with it) the divine mode of recompense, so that therefore (this second כּי signifies also <hi type="italic">nam</hi>, but is, because extending further on account of the first, according to the sense equivalent to <hi type="italic">ita ut</hi>) he has to choose (seek out) another mode of recompense, not Elihu (who is perfectly satisfied with the mode with which history furnishes us); which is then followed by the challenge (דּבּר not <hi type="italic">infin.,</hi> but as <reference osisRef="Job.33.32">Job 33:32</reference>): what (more corresponding to just retribution) thou knowest, speak out then! Elihu on his part knows that he does not stand alone against Job, the censurer of the divine government of the world, but that men of heart (understanding) and (every) wise man who listens to him will coincide with him in the opinion that Job’s talk is devoid of knowledge and intelligence (on the form of writing השׂכּיל as <reference osisRef="Jer.3.15">Jer 3:15</reference>, vid., Ges. §53, rem. 2). <div eID="gen8463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8464" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Job.34.36">Job 34:36</reference> we will for the present leave the meaning of אבי undecided; יבּחן is certainly intended as optative: let Job be tried to the extreme or last, i.e., let his trial by affliction continue until the matter is decided (comp. <reference osisRef="Hab.1.4">Hab 1:4</reference>), on account of the opposition among men of iniquity, i.e., after the manner of such (on this Beth of association comp. בּקּשׁשׁים, <reference osisRef="Job.36.14">Job 36:14</reference>), for to חטּאת, by which the purpose of his affliction is to be cleared up, he adds פּשׁע, viz., the wickedness of blasphemous speeches: among us (therefore without fear) he claps (viz., his hands scornfully together, יספּוק only here thus absolute instead of ישׂפּק כּפּיו fo dae, <reference osisRef="Job.27.23">Job 27:23</reference>, comp. בשׂפק <reference osisRef="Job.36.18">Job 36:18</reference> with ספקו <reference osisRef="Job.20.22">Job 20:22</reference>)<note placement="foot">The mode of writing with ס instead of שׂ is limited in the book of Job, according to the Masora, to <reference osisRef="Job.34.26">Job 34:26</reference>, Job 34:37.</note> and multiplies (ירב, <hi type="italic">fut. apoc. Hiph.</hi> as <reference osisRef="Job.10.17">Job 10:17</reference>, and instead of the full fut., as ישׂר, <reference osisRef="Job.33.27">Job 33:27</reference>) his speeches against God, i.e., exceeds himself in speeches which irreverently dictate to and challenge God. <div eID="gen8464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8465" type="x-p"/> But we now ask, what does that אבי, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.34.36">Job 34:36</reference></hi>, signify? According to the accentuation with <hi type="italic">Rebia</hi>, it appears to be intended to signify <hi type="italic">pater mi</hi> (Jer.), according to which Saad. (<hi type="italic">jâ rabbı̂</hi>) and Gecat. (<hi type="italic">munchiı̂</hi>, my Creator) translate it. This would be the only passage where an Old Testament saint calls God אבי; elsewhere God is called the Father of Israel, and Israel as a people, or the individual comprehending himself with the nation, calls Him אבינו. Nevertheless this <hi type="italic">pater mi</hi> for Elihu would not be inappropriate, for what the writer of the Epistle to the Hebrews, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.7">Heb 12:7</reference>, says to believers on the ground of <reference osisRef="Prov.3.11">Pro 3:11</reference> : εἰς παιδείαν ὑπομένετε, ye suffer for the purpose of paternal discipline, is Elihu’s fundamental thought; he also calls God in <reference osisRef="Job.32.22">Job 32:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.36.3">Job 36:3</reference>, which a like reference to himself, עשׂני and פעלי - this ejaculatory “my Father!” especially in conjunction with the following wish, remains none the less objectionable, and only in the absence of a more agreeable interpretation should we, with Hirz., decide in its favour. It would be disproportionately repulsive if <reference osisRef="Job.34.36">Job 34:36</reference> still belonged to the assenting language of another, and Elihu represented himself as addressed by אבי (Wolfson, Maur.). Thus, therefore, אבי must be taken somehow or other interjectionally. It is untenable to compare it with אבוי, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.29">Pro 23:29</reference>, for אוי ואבוי (Arab. <hi type="italic">âh wa - âwâh</hi>) is “ah! and alas!” The Aramaic בייא בייא, <hi type="italic">vae vae</hi> (Buxtorf, col. 294), compared by Ges. to בּי, signifies just the same. The Targ. translates צבינא, I wish; after which Kimchi, among moderns, Umbr., Schlottm., Carey, and others derive אבי from אבה, a wish (after the form קצה, הזה), but the participial substantival-form badly suits this signification, which is at once improbable according to the usage of the language so far as we at present know it. This interpretation also does not well suit the בי, which is to be explained at the same time. Ewald, §358, <hi type="italic">a</hi>, regards אבי as the fuller form of בּי, and thinks אבי is dialectic = לבי = לוי = לוּ, but this is an etymological leger-demain. The two Schultens (died 1750 and 1793) were on the right track when they traced back אבי to בוא, but their interpretation: <hi type="italic">rem eo adducam ut</hi> (אבי = אביא, as it is certainly not unfrequently written, e.g., 1Ki 21:29, with the assumption of a root בי cognate with בא), is artificial and without support in the usage of the language and in the syntax. Körber and Simonis opened up the right way, but with inadequate means for following it out, by referring (vid., Ges. <hi type="italic">Thes. s.v.</hi> בּי) to the formula of a wish and of respect, <hi type="italic">bawwâk allah ,</hi> which, however, also is <hi type="italic">bajjâk</hi>. The Kamus interprets <hi type="italic">bajjâk</hi>, though waveringly, by <hi type="italic">bawwâk</hi>, the meaning of which (may he give thee a resting-place) is more transparent. In an annotated Codex of Zamachschari <hi type="italic">hajjâk allah wa - bajjâk</hi> is explained: God preserve thy life and grant thee to come to a place of rest, <hi type="italic">bawwaaka</hi> (therefore Arab. <hi type="italic">bawâ</hi> = <hi type="italic">bawa'a</hi>) <hi type="italic">menzilan</hi>. That אבי (as also בּי) is connected with this <hi type="italic">bajjâk</hi> since the latter is the <hi type="italic">Piel</hi>-form of an old verb <hi type="italic">bajja</hi> (vid., <hi type="italic">supra</hi>, p. 559), which with the forms Arab. <hi type="italic">bâ'a</hi> (whence Arab. <hi type="italic">bı̂‛at</hi>, a sheltering house) and Arab. <hi type="italic">bw'</hi> (<hi type="italic">bwâ</hi>) has one root similar in signification with בוא, the following contributions of Wetzstein will show. <div eID="gen8465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8466" type="x-p"/> In elucidation of the present passage he observes: The expressions <hi type="italic">abı̂ tebı̂ , jebı̂ ; nebı̂ , tebû , jebû ,</hi> are so frequent in Damascus, that they very soon struck me, and on my first inquiry I always received the same answer, that they are a mutilation of Arab. <hi type="italic">'bgy , abghi ,</hi> I desire, etc. [<hi type="italic">vid. supra,</hi> p. 580], until one day a fugitive came into the consulate, and with these words, <hi type="italic">abı̂ wâlidêk</hi>, seized me in that part of the body where the Arabs wear the girdle (<hi type="italic">zunnâr</hi>), a symbolic action by which one seeks some one’s protection. Since the word here could not be equivalent to <hi type="italic">abghi</hi> (“I desire” thy parents), I turned to the person best acquainted with the idiom of the country, the scribe <hi type="italic">Abderrahmân</hi> <hi type="italic">el-Mîdâni, </hi>which father had been a wandering minstrel in the camps for twenty years; and he explained to me that <hi type="italic">abghi</hi> only signifies “I desire;” on the contrary, <hi type="italic">abı̂</hi>, “I implore importunately, I pray for God’s sake,” and the latter belongs to a defective verb, Arab. <hi type="italic">bayya</hi>, from which, except the forms mentioned, only the part. <hi type="italic">anâ bâj ,</hi> “I come as a suppliant,” and its plur. <hi type="italic">nahn bâjin ,</hi> is used. The poet <hi type="italic">Musa Rârâ</hi> from <hi type="italic">Krêje</hi> in the south of Hauran, who lived with me six months in Damascus in order to instruct me in the dialect of his district, assured me that among the Beduins also the <hi type="italic">perf</hi>. forms <hi type="italic">bı̂t , bı̂nâ</hi> (I have, we have entreated), and the <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. forms <hi type="italic">tabı̂n</hi> (thou, woman ... ), <hi type="italic">jaben</hi> (they, the women ... ), and <hi type="italic">taben</hi> (ye women ... ), are used. In the year 1858, in the course of a journey in his native country, I came to <hi type="italic">Dîmâs</hi>, whither they had brought two strange Beduins who had been robbed of their horses in that desert (<hi type="italic">Sahra Dîmâs</hi>), and one of them had at the same time received a mortal gunshot-wound. As I can to these men, who were totally forsaken, the wounded man began to express his importunate desire for a surgeon with the words <hi type="italic">jâ shêch nebı̂ ‛arabak</hi>, “Sir, we claim the protection of thy Arabs,” i.e., we adjure thee by thy family. Naturally <hi type="italic">abı̂</hi> occurs most frequently. It generally has its obj. in the <hi type="italic">acc.,</hi> often also with the <hi type="italic">praepos</hi>. Arab. <hi type="italic">‛ly ,</hi> exactly like Arab. <hi type="italic">dchl</hi> (to enter, to flee anywhere and hide), which is its correct synonym and usual substitute in common life. It is often used without an obj., and, indeed, very variously. With women it is chiefly the introduction to a question prompted by curiosity, as: <hi type="italic">abı̂</hi> (ah, tell me), have you really betrothed your daughter? Or the word is accompanied by a gesture by the five fingers of the right hand, with the tips united, being stretched out towards the hasty or impatient listener, as if one wished to show some costly object, when <hi type="italic">abı̂</hi> signifies as much as: I pray thee wait till I have shown thee this precious thing, i.e., allow me to make one more remark to thee in reference to the matter. Moreover, בּי (probably not corrupted from אבי, but a derived <hi type="italic">nomen concretum</hi> in the sense of <hi type="italic">dachı̂ l</hi> or <hi type="italic">mustagı̂r</hi>, one seeking protection, protégé, after the form אי, צי, from בוה = בוא) still exists unaltered in Hauran and in the steppe. The Beduin introduces an important request with the words <hi type="italic">anâ bı̂ ahlak</hi>, I am a protégé of thy family, or <hi type="italic">anâ bı̂ ‛irdak</hi>, I trust to thine honour, etc.; while in Damascus they say, <hi type="italic">anâ dachı̂l ahlak , harı̂mak , aulâdak ,</hi> etc. The Beduin women make use of this <hi type="italic">bı̂</hi> in a weakened signification, in order to beg a piece of soap or sugar, and <hi type="italic">anâ bı̂ lihjetak ,</hi> I pray by thy beard, etc., is often heard. <div eID="gen8466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8467" type="x-p"/> If now we combine that אבי of Elihu with <hi type="italic">abghi</hi> (from Arab. <hi type="italic">bgâ</hi>, Hebr. בּעה, Aram. בּעא, <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. יבעי, as בּי with בּעי) or with <hi type="italic">abî</hi> = אבא, from the verb <hi type="italic">bajja</hi> = בוא (בי),<note placement="foot">We cannot in any case, with Wetzst., explain the אבי אבי,   2Ki 2:12; 2Ki 13:14, according to the above, so that the king of Israel adjured the dying prophet by the national army and army of the faithful not to forsake him, as an Arab is now and then adjured in most urgent and straitened circumstances “by the army of Islam;” vid., on the other hand, 2Ki 6:21, comp. <reference osisRef="Job.5.13">Job 5:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.8.9">Job 8:9</reference> (בּנך). Here rather, if an Arabian parallel be needed, the usual death wail, <hi type="italic">bi - abı̂ anta</hi> (thou wast dear as a father to me), e.g., in Kosegarten, <hi type="italic">Chrestom</hi>. p. 140, 3, is to be compared. אבי,   <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.12">1Sa 24:12</reference>, might more readily, with Ew. §101, <hi type="italic">c</hi>, be brought in here and regarded as belonging to the North Palestine peculiarities of the book of Kings; but by a comparison of the passages cited, this is also improbable.</note> it always remains a remarkable instance in favour of the Arabic colouring of the Elihu section similar to the rest of the book, - a colouring, so to speak, dialectically Hauranitish; while, on the other hand, even by this second speech, one cannot avoid the impression of a great distance between it and the rest of the book: the language has a lofty tone, without its special harshness, as there, being the necessary consequence of a carefully concentrated fulness of thought; moreover, here in general the usual regularity of the strophe-lines no longer prevails, and also the usual symmetrical balance of thought in them. <div eID="gen8467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8468" type="x-p"/> If we confine our attention to the real substance of the speech, apart from the emotional and rough accessories, Elihu casts back the reproach of injustice which Job has raised, first as being contradictory to the being of God, Job 34:10.; then he seeks to refute it as contradicting God’s government, and this he does (1) apagogically from the unselfish love with which God’s protecting care preserves the breath of every living thing, while He who has created all things might bring back all created things to the former non-existence, <reference osisRef="Job.34.12-Job.15.2">Job 34:12-15; (2</reference>) by induction from the impartial judgment which He exercises over princes and peoples, and from which it is inferred that the Ruler of the world is also all-just, <reference osisRef="Job.34.16">Job 34:16</reference>-20. From this Elihu proves that God can exercise justice, and from that, that He is omniscient, and sees into man’s inmost nature without any judicial investigation, <reference osisRef="Job.34.21-Job.34.28">Job 34:21-28</reference>; inaccessible to human accusation and human defiance, He rules over peoples and individuals, even over kings, and nothing turns His just punishment aside but lowly penitence blended with the prayer for the disclosure of unperceived sin, <reference osisRef="Job.34.29">Job 34:29</reference>-32. For in His retributive rule God does not follow the discontented demands of men arrogant and yet devoid of counsel, Job 34:33. It is worthy of recognition, that Elihu does not here coincide with what has been already said (especially <reference osisRef="Job.12.15">Job 12:15</reference>), without applying it to another purpose; and that his theodicy differs essentially from that proclaimed by the friends. It is not derived from mere appearance, but lays hold of the very principles. It does not attempt the explanation of the many apparent contradictions to retributive justice which outward events manifest, as agreeing with it; it does not solve the question by mere empiricism, but from the idea of the Godhead and its relation to the world, and by such inner necessity guarantees to the mysteries still remaining to human shortsightedness, their future solution.  <chapter eID="Job.34"/> <div eID="gen8468" type="x-p"/>

( jâ rabbı̂ ) and Gecat. ( munchiı̂ , my Creator) translate it.
